title: Infra GPU fleet: capacity, cloud accounts, IaC modules, and CI/CD playbook
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview

This document consolidates best practices, guardrails, and runbooks for Redwood Inference's infra team responsible for the GPU fleet, cloud accounts and networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD and build pipelines, and day-2 runbooks. It is intended for engineers operating and evolving the fleet (oncall, infra owners, and SREs).

Scope

- Fleet sizing and capacity planning for hosted and dedicated clusters.
- Cloud account setup and network baseline for GPU workloads.
- Terraform/IaC module standards and recommended module list.
- CI/CD pipeline templates for module testing and cluster deploys.
- Runbooks for common operational incidents and day-2 maintenance.

Ownership and stakeholders

- Primary owner: infra-engineering (gpu-fleet subteam).
- SRE: oncall rotation for gpu-fleet incidents.
- Networking: vpc-and-networking team for baseline network ACLs and peering.
- Security: security-and-compliance for KMS, secrets, and audit requirements.

Key Concepts and Terminology

- GPU node: VM/instance with 1+ attached GPU. Example types: A100-80GB, H100-80GB, and T4 for inference.
- Pool: logical grouping of GPU nodes (e.g., host-api-pool, batch-infer-pool, dedicated-customer-POOL).
- Buffer capacity: reserved idle capacity to preserve SLOs during spikes (recommended 10%-25%).
- Continuous batching: runtime feature that prefers slightly higher utilization while meeting latency SLOs.

Capacity planning guidance

1. SLOs and targets

- Latency SLO: P95 <= 120ms for hosted text-generation small (<= 512 tokens) workloads.
- Throughput target: maintain >= 85% of provisioned throughput for cost-effectiveness.
- Buffer target: maintain 10%-20% spare GPU capacity for regional failover and rolling upgrades.

2. Inputs for sizing model

- Request distribution by model type and sequence length.
- Average tokens per request and per-minute request rates.
- Model-specific GPU utilization profiles (from model onboarding perf profiles).

3. Example sizing calculation (summary)

- Baseline sustained request rate: 12k requests/min for small-model production.
- Average effective qps per GPU (A100-80GB) for small-model: 45 qps.
- Required GPUs = ceil(12,000 / 45) = 267 GPUs.
- Add buffer 15% -> 307 GPUs provisioned.

GPU types and placement strategy

- Mixed fleet strategy: newer high-efficiency GPUs (H100) for high-throughput/low-latency routes; older A100s for mixed workloads; T4s for low-cost embedding and batch workloads.
- Placement rules: prefer same-GPU type within a pool; fall back to compatible variants via runtime smart-routing.

Cloud accounts and networking baseline

- Account structure:
  - org-root (master billing)
  - infra-prod (hosting production clusters and shared services)
  - infra-stage (staging/preprod)
  - customer-dedicated-<customer-id> (for Dedicated deployments with isolated accounts)

- Networking baseline (VPC):
  - Private subnets for GPU nodes, with NAT gateways in dedicated egress subnets.
  - Transit/peering for cross-account control-plane access (control plane in infra-prod account).
  - Security groups: restrict ports to telemetry (9090), health (8080), SSH only via bastion with short-lived certs.
  - Flow logs enabled (retain 90 days by default for infra teams; extended retention for security reviews).

Terraform / IaC modules (standards and recommended modules)

Standards:
- All modules must be versioned and published to our private module registry.
- Modules must include examples/, test/ (unit/integration), and a changelog in README.md.
- Provide a stable interface: avoid breaking changes to module inputs without a major version bump.

Recommended modules (name -> responsibility):
- infra-gpu-cluster: create autoscaling groups, instance profiles, bootstrap scripts, and driver installation.
- infra-gpu-networking: VPC, subnets, route tables, NAT gateways, and peering attachments.
- infra-iam-gpu: IAM roles, instance profiles, and cross-account role bindings.
- infra-k8s-nodegroup: Nodegroup and kubelet bootstrap configuration for managed k8s (if used).
- infra-secrets-kms: KMS keys, key rotation policy, and grants for service principals.
- infra-monitoring-agent: Prometheus/agent deployment configuration and exporter configs.

Example module usage (terraform snippet):

```
module "gpu_cluster" {
  source = "registry.redwood/internal/infra-gpu-cluster/aws"
  version = "v2.3.0"

  name_prefix     = "hosted-api"
  gpu_instance_type = "nvidia-a100-80gb"
  min_size        = 30
  max_size        = 350
  desired_capacity = 120
  ssh_key_name    = var.ssh_key_name
  tags = {
    team = "infra-engineering"
    env  = "prod"
  }
}
```

Module testing and QA

- All module changes must pass: unit tests (tftest), static checks (tflint, tfsec), and CI plan validation against a mocked state.
- Integration tests must run against a staging account with ephemeral resources.
- Release process: tag -> CI builds module artifact -> publish to private registry -> create PR to update consumers.

CI/CD and build pipelines

Pipeline templates and conventions:
- Repo layout: modules/ | pipelines/ | examples/ | tests/
- Branch protection: main requires PR with passing CI and 2 reviewers.
- CI steps (modules repo):
  1. Checkout + setup Terraform version manager (tfenv).
  2. Run tflint, tfsec, fmt; fail on errors.
  3. Run tftest unit suite.
  4. Run terraform plan in a sandboxed staging project (requires ephemeral creds).
  5. If release tag, publish module and notify downstream owners.

Cluster deploy pipelines (infra-apps):
- Canary rollout: deploy 1-2 nodes into canary pool, run smoke tests (latency, model health), then gradually scale.
- Blue/green for control-plane changes (egress, IAM binding, DNS updates).

CD triggers and gating:
- Automated scaling policies change via PR must include cost and SLO impact assessment.
- Any network or IAM change requires security review (label "security-review") and must be signed off by security.

Runbooks and operational playbooks

Incident: GPU node depletion (high pending requests)

1. Symptoms:
  - Queueing increases, p99 latency spikes, autoscaler not adding nodes, or cloud quota errors.
2. Immediate actions:
  - Check autoscaler logs: kubectl -n kube-system logs deployment/cluster-autoscaler --since=15m.
  - Verify cloud quotas: aws service-quotas get-service-quota --service-code ec2 --quota-code L-1216C47A (example command).
  - Check GPU-driver/agent health: kubectl get pods -n gpu-system -l app=gpu-agent -o wide.
3. Remediation steps (order):
  1. If autoscaler errors: restart autoscaler pod and inspect recent events.
  2. If cloud quota hit: open quota increase request and temporarily scale down noncritical pools (batch/embeddings).
  3. If driver failure: cordon affected nodes and roll the node-driver DaemonSet (kubectl rollout restart ds/gpu-driver -n gpu-system).
4. Post-incident:
  - Run RCA template and update capacity model if traffic forecast caused the incident.

Incident: Network impact on cluster pods (service networking failures)

- Quick checks:
  - Verify VPC route tables and NAT gateway metrics.
  - Ensure security groups did not change.
  - Confirm peering connections and transit gateway attachments are UP.

Scheduled maintenance and day-2 ops

- Rolling kernel/driver upgrades: ensure a 10%-15% extra buffer before maintenance window.
- OS image and security patching: use baked AMI images and staged canary rollouts.
- Capacity refresh plan (quarterly): review model profiles, retire low-efficiency GPUs, and plan procurement.

Change rollout checklist (pre-merge for any infra change affecting fleet)

1. Include a short description of impact and rollout steps in PR.
2. Cost impact estimate (monthly delta).
3. SLO/regression test plan with smoke tests.
4. Security review (if IAM/networking/secrets affected).
5. Assign oncall engineer for the rollout window.

Monitoring, alerts, and dashboards

- Key metrics:
  - GPU utilization (per type and per-pool).
  - Pending requests / queue length.
  - Node health (driver crash loop, GPU ECC errors).
  - Autoscaler decision latency.
  - Cloud quotas and billing alerts (forecast vs actual).

- Priority alerts:
  - Critical: >20% of pool nodes NotReady OR queue growth > 2x baseline for 5m.
  - High: P95 latency > 150% of SLO for 5m.
  - Medium: sustained GPU utilization > 95% for 30m (suspiciously high).

Troubleshooting checklist (quick commands)

- kube-events: kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp | tail -n 200
- pod/logs: kubectl -n <ns> logs <pod> -c <container> --since=10m
- node-status: kubectl get nodes -o wide; kubectl describe node <node>
- cloud-instances: aws ec2 describe-instances --filters Name=tag:cluster,Values=hosted-api

Security and compliance notes

- All production keys must use KMS with key rotation enabled.
- Audit logging: enable control-plane and flow logs; store evidence for 12 months for regulated customers.
- Access: SSH to nodes only via short-lived bastion sessions using OIDC-based certs.

Frequently asked operational questions

Q: When should we add a new GPU type to the fleet?
A: Add when the new type shows >20% cost-efficiency improvement for a representative workload and we have at least one large customer/route that benefits. Run a pilot in staging for at least two weeks.

Q: How much buffer should Dedicated pools keep versus hosted pools?
A: Dedicated pools should keep a smaller buffer (5-10%) because of predictable commits; hosted pools should keep 10-20% buffer.

Appendix: Example escalation matrix

- Pager: oncall-gpu (primary) -> infra-lead (30m) -> eng-sre-manager (60m)
- Slack channels: #infra-gpu (incident comms), #security (if credentials/keys implicated)

Related links and references

- Internal module registry: https://registry.redwood.internal/modules
- Perf profiles: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding
- Capacity calculator notebook: /repos/infra/capacity/calc-notebooks/README.md

Document maintenance

- Owner (infra-engineering) must review quarterly or after any capacity incident.
- Update this playbook when new GPU families or cloud account structure changes are approved.
summary: Consolidated playbook for GPU fleet capacity, cloud accounts, Terraform modules, CI/CD, and runbooks for infra engineers.
